## What Lecture 3.1 Left Unasked

Lecture 3.1 put ability into the earnings equation. The return to schooling fell
from 1.6700 to 1.2538, and we could say why: ability raises schooling and ability
raises pay, so the short regression attributed both to schooling.

That was an argument about which variables belong. It left the variables
themselves alone. Every equation this module has written, from 2.1 onwards, says
that the tenth year of schooling and the twentieth are each worth the same 1.30
euro to the same person.

::: {.defn title="Question"}
Which lecture decided that? And is it a claim about the Irish labour market, or
a claim about a straight line?
:::

## Lecture Plan

::: {.contributions}
1.  **Logs and Elasticities.** Take the log of a variable and its coefficient answers a different question, in proportions rather than euro.
2.  **Dummy Variables.** A category enters as a 0/1 column and shifts the intercept, relative to a base category you chose.
3.  **Interactions.** Let the slope differ across two groups, and the coefficient on schooling stops meaning what it meant.
:::

# Logs and Elasticities

## One Euro Figure at Every Level of Schooling

```{=latex}
\fig{../_shared/placeholder.pdf}{The same 120 people twice: earnings on schooling, then log earnings on schooling.}
```

::: {.tablenotes title="Two Straight Lines, Two Different Claims About Ireland"}
The left panel says each extra year adds the same euro figure at every level. The
right panel says each extra year raises earnings by the same proportion, so its
euro value rises as schooling rises. Neither is more natural than the other.
:::

## Logs Put the Return in Proportional Terms

To ask what a year of schooling is worth as a proportion of what a person already
earns, put the logarithm on the left-hand side:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\log(w_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 (S_i - 13) + u_i
\end{equation}
```

- $w_i$: hourly earnings of person $i$, in euro
- $\log(\cdot)$: the natural logarithm
- $S_i$: years of schooling, centred at thirteen
- $\beta_1$: the rise in log earnings per year of schooling
- $u_i$: everything other than schooling

A one-year rise in schooling adds $\beta_1$ to log earnings, and
$100\,\Delta\log(w) \approx \%\Delta w$, so $100\beta_1$ is a percentage
[@wooldridge2020, eq. A.23 p.675]. Fitted here, $\hat{\beta}_1 = 0.1481$ with a
standard error of 0.0239, so the shortcut reads 14.81 per cent per year and the
exact figure is $100(e^{0.1481}-1) = 15.96$ per cent.

::: {.defn title="Semi-Elasticity"}
$\beta_1$ maps an ABSOLUTE change in schooling to a PROPORTIONAL change in
earnings, so it is a semi-elasticity, and $100\beta_1$ is the percentage rise per
year [@wooldridge2020, eq. 2.43 p.37].
:::

## Why a Log-Log Slope Is an Elasticity

Put the logarithm on both sides and the slope is unit-free. An elasticity is
defined as a ratio of proportional changes, so derive the slope from that
definition rather than asserting the name:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\gamma_1
  &= \frac{d\log(w)}{d\log(S)}
   = \frac{d w / w}{d S / S}
   \qquad\text{because } \frac{d\log(x)}{dx} = \frac{1}{x}
   \\[4pt]
  &= \frac{dw}{dS}\cdot\frac{S}{w}
   = \frac{\%\Delta w}{\%\Delta S}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
```

- $\gamma_1$: the elasticity of earnings with respect to schooling

The first line rewrites each differential of a log as a proportional change. The
second cancels the levels, and what is left has euro over euro on top and years
over years underneath. Both units divide out, which is why an elasticity has none
[@wooldridge2020, eq. A.24 p.676, and p.679]. Fitted here,
$\hat{\gamma}_1 = 2.0119$ with a standard error of 0.3185: one per cent more
schooling goes with about 2.01 per cent more earnings, in euro, cents, years or
months alike.

## Four Specifications and How to Read Each One

```{=latex}
\tabcaption{The same two variables under four specifications, and the sentence each slope supports.}

\begin{dgtable}{p{0.13\linewidth} p{0.13\linewidth} p{0.13\linewidth} p{0.45\linewidth}}
\thead{Specification} & \thead{Regression} & \thead{Change in $S$} & \thead{Say this out loud} \\
\midrule
Level--level & $w$ on $S$ & one year & One more year of schooling adds
  $\beta_1$ euro to hourly earnings. \\
Level--log   & $w$ on $\log S$ & one per cent & One per cent more schooling
  adds $\beta_1/100$ euro to hourly earnings. \\
Log--level   & $\log w$ on $S$ & one year & One more year of schooling raises
  earnings by about $100\beta_1$ per cent. \\
Log--log     & $\log w$ on $\log S$ & one per cent & One per cent more schooling
  raises earnings by about $\beta_1$ per cent. \\
\end{dgtable}

\dgnotes{Only the first row is exact. The word ``about'' in the other three is
the approximation $100\,\Delta\log x \approx \%\Delta x$, made precise two frames
from here.}
```

The four rows are Wooldridge's Table 2.3 [@wooldridge2020, p.39]. Our four fitted
slopes are 1.5227, 19.7087, 0.1481 and 2.0119, in that order, and not one of them
can be compared with the one above it. Write the log-log sentence out in full
before the next frame: if it contains the word euro, or the word year, you have
described one of the other three rows.

## Per Cent and Percentage Point Are Not the Same Word

A percentage change is measured relative to where you started. A percentage point
is the plain arithmetic difference between two percentages. When the variable is
itself a rate, both are available and they are different numbers:

- A sales tax rising from 4 per cent to 6 per cent is a rise of **two percentage points**.
- The same rise is $100 \times (6-4)/4 = 50.0000$ **per cent**, because the base is 4.
- Michigan voters were told both figures in 1994, and both were correct [@wooldridge2020, p.672].

For a variable measured in euro there is no ambiguity, because earnings are not a
percentage and a percentage point change in them is undefined.

::: {.caveat title="What This Costs When the Dependent Variable Is a Rate"}
Regress an unemployment rate on schooling in levels and the coefficient is in
percentage points. Regress its logarithm and the coefficient is a percentage
change of the rate itself. Unemployment going from 8 to 9 is one percentage point
and a 12.5 per cent rise [@wooldridge2020, p.188].
:::

## The Exact Percentage Change and When the Shortcut Fails

The shortcut $100\beta_1$ is an approximation. Difference the fitted model across
a one-year rise in schooling and exponentiate, and the exact figure appears
[@wooldridge2020, eq. 6.9 p.186]:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\%\Delta w = 100\bigl(e^{\beta_1} - 1\bigr)
\end{equation}
```

```{=latex}
\tabcaption{The shortcut against the exact figure, computed at four values of the coefficient.}

\begin{dgtable}{p{0.16\linewidth} p{0.22\linewidth} p{0.22\linewidth} p{0.22\linewidth}}
\thead{$\beta_1$} & \thead{Shortcut $100\beta_1$} & \thead{Exact} & \thead{Gap} \\
\midrule
0.05 & 5.0000  & 5.1271  & 0.1271  \\
0.10 & 10.0000 & 10.5171 & 0.5171  \\
0.25 & 25.0000 & 28.4025 & 3.4025  \\
0.50 & 50.0000 & 64.8721 & 14.8721 \\
\end{dgtable}

\dgnotes{Pure arithmetic about the exponential function, to four decimal places.
The gap grows with the square of $\beta_1$, so it quadruples when $\beta_1$
doubles.}
```

Below about 0.10 the shortcut is off by a tenth of a percentage point and
everyone uses it. At 0.50 it understates by nearly fifteen, which rewrites a
sentence in a results section. It understates in every row, and always will.

## What Logs Cost: One of Our Own 120 People

The logarithm is undefined at zero and below, and the lowest earner in our
standing sample is on $-0.06$ euro an hour. Every log specification on this deck
is therefore fitted on **119 people, not 120**:

- The level-level slope, 1.5227, uses all 120 of them.
- The log-level slope, 0.1481, and the log-log slope, 2.0119, use 119.
- The person dropped is the poorest one, which is rarely the person you can spare.

Adding a euro before taking the log would keep them, but that constant sets the
answer and is a choice about units rather than a repair. Years of schooling stay
unlogged throughout, because a year is already a natural unit
[@wooldridge2020, p.187].

::: {.caveat title="Our Population Was Generated as a Straight Line"}
The 200,000 people were built with a constant 1.30 euro return and a normal
error, which is what puts one of them below zero. A log specification fitted to
them is a shape we imposed, and it still fits: $R^2$ is 0.2476 for the log-level
model against 0.3531 for the level-level one. Those two figures are not
comparable, because they account for variation in two different dependent
variables [@wooldridge2020, p.188], and Lecture 3.3 returns to that.
:::

## A Training Coefficient of 0.08

A regression of log earnings on a training dummy returns 0.08. A colleague writes
that training raises earnings by eight percentage points.

::: {.defn title="Question"}
Two separate errors are stacked in that sentence. Name both, and give the figure
the sentence should have carried.
:::

# Dummy Variables

## A Category Enters the Model as an Intercept Shift

To put something that is not a number into a regression, code it as a column of
ones and zeros and let it move the intercept. Today's group is graduates,
sixteen years of schooling or more: 19 of our 120 people:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
w_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 (S_i - 13) + \delta\, G_i + u_i
\end{equation}
```

- $G_i$: one if person $i$ has sixteen or more years of schooling, zero otherwise
- $\delta$: the vertical gap between graduates and non-graduates

Set $G_i = 0$ and the intercept is $\beta_0$; set $G_i = 1$ and it is
$\beta_0 + \delta$. The slope on schooling is $\beta_1$ either way, so the two
fitted lines are parallel and $\delta$ is the same gap at every level of
schooling [@wooldridge2020, eq. 7.1 p.222].

::: {.defn title="Delta Is a Difference Between Two Conditional Means"}
$\delta = E[w \mid G = 1, S] - E[w \mid G = 0, S]$, with schooling held at the
same value in both terms [@wooldridge2020, eq. 7.2 p.222]. Nothing about least
squares is different: one more column, and only its reading is new.
:::

## Two Parallel Lines Through One Sample

```{=latex}
\fig{../_shared/placeholder.pdf}{Graduates against non-graduates, with two parallel fitted lines and the 2.8634 gap marked.}
```

::: {.tablenotes title="The Vertical Gap Is the Coefficient, and It Never Widens"}
The two lines are parallel by construction, because the model gave both groups
the same coefficient on schooling, 1.2042. If the gap in the data widens or
narrows with schooling, this model cannot report that, and section 3 is the
repair.
:::

<!-- FIGURE 3-2_dummy: one scatter of the standing 120, points coloured by the
     graduate dummy (19 graduates, 101 non-graduates), two parallel fitted lines
     in the theme palette. The vertical gap must be annotated as delta = 2.8634
     with a double-headed arrow, drawn at the sample mean of schooling, 13.4473,
     NOT at zero. Same colours and point identities as 3-2_interaction. -->

## The Coefficient Is a Difference Between Two Averages

Take schooling out of that model and leave the intercept and the dummy. Least
squares then has two parameters and two groups, so it reproduces each group's
mean exactly. Our 101 non-graduates average 10.9550 and our 19 graduates average
19.1277, a difference of 8.1726:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\hat{w}_i = \underbrace{10.9550}_{\text{non-graduate mean}}
  + \underbrace{8.1726}_{\text{difference of the two means}} G_i
  \qquad \mathrm{se}(\hat{\delta}) = 1.2806
\end{equation}
```

Both fitted coefficients match the two averages to four decimal places, which is
not a coincidence [@wooldridge2020, p.224]. So a constant and one dummy are the
comparison anyone would have made without regression at all.

::: {.takeaway title="Schooling Cuts the Graduate Premium From 8.17 to 2.86"}
Put schooling back and $\hat{\delta}$ falls to 2.8634, with a standard error of
1.6594, while the slope on schooling is 1.2042. Most of the raw gap was schooling
itself: graduates have more of it. That is Lecture 3.1's partialling out with a
0/1 column in place of a continuous one [@angrist2015].
:::

## Every Dummy Coefficient Is a Comparison Against the Omitted Category

A graduate dummy has two categories. Highest qualification has five: Leaving
Certificate, apprenticeship, certificate, degree, postgraduate. Four dummies go
in and the software prints four numbers:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
w_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 (S_i - 13)
   + \delta_1 Q_{1i} + \delta_2 Q_{2i} + \delta_3 Q_{3i} + \delta_4 Q_{4i} + u_i
\end{equation}
```

- $Q_{ji}$: one if person $i$ holds qualification $j$, zero otherwise
- $\delta_j$: the gap between qualification $j$ and the omitted one

Every one of the four is a comparison against the category you left out
[@wooldridge2020, p.229]. Reset the base and all four printed numbers change
while nothing about Ireland does. In R the base is the first level of the factor,
which is alphabetical unless `relevel()` says otherwise, so spelling can decide
what your table reports.

::: {.caveat title="The Sentence a Table of Dummies Needs Underneath It"}
Name the omitted category in the note under the table. Without it a reader cannot
attach a meaning to any of the four numbers, and $\delta_2 - \delta_3$ is the only
route to a gap between two categories that are both in the model. Our simulated
people carry years of schooling and no qualification label, so this frame is
about the shape of the table rather than about our 120.
:::

## Why One Category Must Be Left Out

Put in a dummy for every one of the five qualifications as well as an intercept.
Each person holds exactly one, so $\sum_{j=1}^{5} Q_{ji} = 1$ for every person,
which is the intercept column exactly. Now shift the coefficients by any constant
$c$:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
(\beta_0 + c) + \sum_{j=1}^{5} (\delta_j - c) Q_{ji}
  = \beta_0 + \sum_{j=1}^{5} \delta_j Q_{ji}
  \;-\; c\Bigl(\underbrace{\textstyle\sum_{j=1}^{5} Q_{ji}}_{=\,1} - 1\Bigr)
\end{equation}
```

The bracket is zero for every person, so every fitted value, every residual and
the residual sum of squares are all unchanged. Infinitely many coefficient
vectors fit identically well, so no unique least squares answer exists.

::: {.defn title="The Dummy Variable Trap"}
This is assumption three of Lecture 3.1, no perfect collinearity, failing exactly
rather than nearly [@wooldridge2020, MLR.3 p.80]. With $g$ categories and an
intercept, $g-1$ dummies go in. R drops one and prints the rest without comment.
:::

## Dummy Coefficients When Earnings Are Logged

With $\log(w)$ on the left, a dummy coefficient is a proportional gap and the
same two readings apply, the shortcut and the exact figure
[@wooldridge2020, eq. 7.10 p.227]:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\text{shortcut: } 100\hat{\delta}
\qquad\qquad
\text{exact: } 100\bigl(e^{\hat{\delta}} - 1\bigr)
\end{equation}
```

At $\hat{\delta} = 0.08$ the shortcut gives 8.0000 and the exact figure is
8.3287, because $\log(1.08) = 0.0770$ and a coefficient of 0.0770 is what an
8.00 per cent gap actually produces. At $\hat{\delta} = -0.297$ Wooldridge's own
wage equation reads 29.7 per cent as a shortcut and 25.7 per cent exactly
[@wooldridge2020, p.227].

::: {.caveat title="Why the Shortcut Is Still Worth Printing"}
Reverse the base group and the exact figure is not the same number: the gap the
other way round is 34.6 per cent, not 25.7. The shortcut, 29.7, sits between the
two, so it is the one figure that does not require you to choose a direction
first [@wooldridge2020, p.228].
:::

## Three Qualification Coefficients and No Base Named

A table reports coefficients on `apprenticeship`, `degree` and `postgraduate`.
Your co-author writes that the degree coefficient is the return to a degree.

::: {.defn title="Question"}
What is that number a comparison against, and what else must the table print
before any sentence about it can be written?
:::

# Interactions

## Interaction Terms Let the Slope Differ Across Groups

Nothing so far lets the return to schooling differ between two groups. Add the
product of schooling and the dummy as one more column:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
w_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 (S_i - 13) + \delta\, G_i + \gamma (S_i - 13)G_i + u_i
\end{equation}
```

- $(S_i - 13)G_i$: the product of the two, one variable, one column
- $\gamma$: the difference in slope between graduates and non-graduates

The product is zero for everyone with $G_i = 0$ and equals centred schooling for
everyone else, which is why it can sit beside both parent terms without repeating
either [@wooldridge2020, eq. 7.17 p.233].

::: {.defn title="Both Parent Terms Stay In"}
The equal-slopes claim is $H_0: \gamma = 0$, and it is a claim about the slope
only: a gap between the groups is still allowed under it
[@wooldridge2020, p.234]. Dropping $G_i$ or $(S_i-13)$ tests something nobody
asked about.
:::

## Two Fitted Lines That Are Not Parallel

```{=latex}
\fig{../_shared/placeholder.pdf}{The same two groups, now with two fitted lines whose slopes are allowed to differ.}
```

::: {.tablenotes title="The Difference in Slope Is the Interaction Coefficient"}
The vertical gap between the lines is no longer one number. It narrows as
schooling rises, and the rate at which it does so is $\gamma = -1.2068$. The
graduate line is nearly flat, and the next two frames say both what that means
and how little the 120 people settle it.
:::

<!-- FIGURE 3-2_interaction: same scatter, same colours and same point
     identities as 3-2_dummy, so the two slides read as one argument. Two
     non-parallel fitted lines, slopes 1.2599 and 0.0531. Annotate the slope
     difference as gamma = -1.2068, and mark the vertical gap at 13 years AND at
     18 years so the two are visibly different. Draw a light vertical reference
     line at 13. The graduate line is fitted on 19 points and should carry a
     confidence band so its width is visible against the other. -->

## What the Schooling Coefficient Means Once an Interaction Is In

Substitute the two values of the dummy into the model and read the slope off each
line:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
G_i = 0:\quad \hat{w}_i &= 11.2710 + 1.2599\,(S_i - 13) \\[2pt]
G_i = 1:\quad \hat{w}_i &= (11.2710 + 7.6357) + (1.2599 - 1.2068)(S_i - 13)
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
```

So the return is 1.2599 euro a year for non-graduates and
$1.2599 - 1.2068 = 0.0531$ for graduates, and $\hat{\gamma} = -1.2068$ is the
difference between them [@wooldridge2020, eq. 7.16 p.233].

Before the interaction, 1.2042 was the return for everybody. After it, 1.2599 is
the return for non-graduates alone. It is not an average of the two, it is not
the overall return, and the printout will not warn you that its meaning is now
narrower.

::: {.caveat title="This Misreading Is Not a Student Error"}
It is the most common error in published work using interactions. The coefficient
on a main term is a partial effect evaluated at one value of the other regressor,
and with a dummy that value is zero, meaning the base group
[@wooldridge2020, p.193].
:::

## Why Centring Schooling Makes the Intercept Interpretable

Run the same model on raw schooling instead of centred schooling, and take the
difference between the two groups at a given $S_i$:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\text{raw scale:}\quad
  E[w \mid G=1, S] - E[w \mid G=0, S] &= \delta + \gamma S_i \\[2pt]
\text{centred:}\quad
  E[w \mid G=1, S] - E[w \mid G=0, S] &= \delta + \gamma (S_i - 13)
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
```

On the raw scale $\delta$ is the gap at $S_i = 0$, which is nobody: no one in the
population has zero years of schooling. On the centred scale $\hat{\delta} =
7.6357$ is the gap at thirteen years, the Leaving Certificate, and
$\hat{\beta}_0 = 11.2710$ is expected hourly earnings there for a non-graduate.

::: {.takeaway title="Centring Relocates Two Coefficients and Nothing Else"}
Every fitted value, every residual and $\gamma$ itself are identical under both
[@wooldridge2020, p.193]. Centring is not a statistical repair. It reports two of
the coefficients at a point you can defend, and their standard errors at that
point come with them.
:::

## The Standard Error of the Slope for the Other Group

Reading 1.2599 and 0.0531 off a table and concluding that the two groups differ
is the error this lecture exists to prevent. The claim is about $\gamma$, so it
has to be tested on $\gamma$.

The return for graduates is $\hat{\beta}_1 + \hat{\gamma}$, and the spread of a
sum is not the sum of the spreads. Lecture 1.2's algebra of variances gives:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1 + \hat{\gamma})
  = \operatorname{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1)
  + \operatorname{Var}(\hat{\gamma})
  + 2\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\beta}_1, \hat{\gamma})
\end{equation}
```

- $\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\beta}_1, \hat{\gamma})$: how the two estimates miss together across samples

That covariance is not on the printout, so the standard error cannot be assembled
from the two printed ones. Refit with graduates as the base and read
$\hat{\beta}_1 + \hat{\gamma}$ straight off, with its standard error attached
[@wooldridge2020, p.194, p.229].

::: {.caveat title="1.2599 Against 0.0531, and t Equal to Minus 0.96"}
The two fitted slopes look nothing alike, and the difference between them is not
distinguishable from zero: $\hat{\gamma} = -1.2068$ has a standard error of
1.2566, so $t = -0.96$ and Lecture 2.4's rule does not reject equal slopes. An
interaction is estimated off a difference between two subgroup slopes, one of
them fitted on 19 people, so it is far less precise than either.
:::

## The Return to Schooling for Women

Log earnings on centred schooling, a dummy for women, and their interaction. You
are asked for the return to schooling for women.

::: {.defn title="Question"}
Which of the three coefficients answers it, and how would you obtain the standard
error that belongs beside your answer?
:::

## What Would Have To Be True?

This time the question is asked of the shape, not of a number. The straight line,
the logarithm and the graduate cut at sixteen years were all chosen by us before
anything was fitted, and the graduate dummy is built out of schooling itself, so
the two groups barely overlap in it.

::: {.defn title="Question"}
What would have to be true for this number to mean what we just said it means?
And what is the plausible story where it isn't?
:::

## Application

Fit all four specifications to the same people and write each slope out as a
sentence with units before reading the next one. Level-level gives 1.5227 with
$R^2 = 0.3531$; level-log 19.7087 with 0.3309; log-level 0.1481 with 0.2476;
log-log 2.0119 with 0.2543. The last two are fitted on 119 people.

::: {.defn title="Question"}
Answer before anything is run. Which of the four will report the highest $R^2$,
and does the winner tell you which shape generated the data?
:::

The lab adds `log()`, `factor()` and `relevel()`, and `y ~ x * d` as shorthand for
a model carrying both parent terms and their product.


All four are drawn on the level scale so that they can be compared at all. The

## Summary: Logs, Dummies and Interactions

::: {.contributions}
1.  **Logs and Elasticities.** A log puts the coefficient in proportions: 0.1481 per year, 2.0119 per cent per cent, and one of our 120 people dropped.
2.  **Dummy Variables.** A dummy shifts the intercept by a difference in two means, 8.1726 raw and 2.8634 once schooling is held fixed.
3.  **Interactions.** The product term lets the slope differ, 1.2599 against 0.0531, and $t = -0.96$ says our 120 people do not settle that.
:::

## Next Lecture

Today produced a block of four qualification dummies and an interaction with
$t = -0.96$, and no tool for deciding whether either belongs. Lecture 3.3
supplies it:

- **Testing Restrictions:** asking about four coefficients at once, which four separate t-statistics cannot do.
- **Choosing a Specification:** what adjusted $R^2$ charges for a column, and why 0.3531 and 0.2476 are not a comparison.
- **Multicollinearity:** what correlated columns do to a standard error, which is where today's 1.2566 comes from.

The first question in 3.3 is which coefficient gives the gap between two
qualifications that are both in the model.

## {.plain}

## Derivation: Where the Exact Percentage Change Comes From

The body frame stated $\%\Delta w = 100(e^{\beta_1}-1)$. It is the fitted model
differenced across one year and exponentiated:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\log \hat{w}(S+1) - \log \hat{w}(S) = \beta_1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{\hat{w}(S+1)}{\hat{w}(S)} = e^{\beta_1}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{\Delta \hat{w}}{\hat{w}} = e^{\beta_1} - 1
\end{equation}
```

::: {.takeaway title="The Shortcut Is the First Term of a Series"}
$e^{\beta_1} - 1 = \beta_1 + \beta_1^2/2 + \dots$, so the shortcut drops
everything past the first term and the leading error is $\beta_1^2/2$. That is
0.00125 at $\beta_1 = 0.05$ and 0.125 at $\beta_1 = 0.50$, which is the shape of
the gap column on the body frame [@wooldridge2020, p.186].
:::

## Derivation: Why the Centring Constant Cancels From the Slopes

Replacing $S_i$ by $S_i - 13$ throughout rewrites the intercept and the dummy
coefficient and leaves both slopes alone:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\beta_0^{\text{raw}} + \beta_1 S_i + \delta^{\text{raw}} G_i + \gamma S_i G_i
  = \underbrace{(\beta_0^{\text{raw}} + 13\beta_1)}_{\beta_0}
  + \beta_1 (S_i - 13)
  + \underbrace{(\delta^{\text{raw}} + 13\gamma)}_{\delta} G_i
  + \gamma (S_i - 13) G_i
\end{equation}
```

::: {.takeaway title="Two Coefficients Are Relabelled, Two Are Not"}
$\beta_1$ and $\gamma$ appear unchanged on both sides, so no slope, fitted value
or residual differs. Only the intercept and the dummy coefficient are relabelled,
which is the whole of what centring does [@wooldridge2020, p.193].
:::

## Notes and Tools

- **The App:** the specification app, with the four forms and the interaction switchable.
- **The Lecture in One Line:** `lm(log(w) ~ I(S - 13) * D)`, which carries both parent terms.
- **This Lecture's Lab:** `log()`, `factor()`, `relevel()`, and `I(S - 13)` for centring without touching the data.
